web_evidence.title: Backlash Realism: The American Novel during the Long 1980s
web_evidence.note: This Tufts doctoral dissertation identifies Charlie Schuyler's first-person perspective, Burr's memoirs and journals as embedded texts, and Burr overall as heavily framed first-person narration(s).

web_evidence.title: Gore Vidal Writing Styles in Burr
web_evidence.note: The point-of-view analysis explicitly states that Charlie narrates in first person and that Aaron Burr also narrates his memoirs in first person.

web_evidence.title: Before There Was “Hamilton,” There Was “Burr”
web_evidence.note: Smithsonian describes the novel as a story within a story, identifies Charles Schuyler as narrator, and identifies Burr's reminiscences as the book's second narrative; its cited examples expose first-person voices in both layers.

web_evidence.title: Gore Vidal Criticism: Vidal, Gore (Vol. 4)
web_evidence.note: The page reprints contemporary criticism explicitly describing the fictional biographer as a first-person narrator and Burr's own account as first-person narrative.

person_note: The novel uses two sustained but consistently first-person narrative voices: fictional journalist Charlie Schuyler in the 1830s frame and Aaron Burr in the constitutive memoir sections. The many narratorial I, me, my, us, and we passages in the quotes independently corroborate the scholarly whole-book structural account. Third-person descriptions of Jefferson, Burr, and other figures are therefore unmarked locally rather than evidence of third-person base narration, while pronouns confined to dialogue and aphorisms are non-base. Because multiple narrators remain in the same grammatical person, the result is FIRST rather than ALTERNATING. The main residual uncertainty is assigning a few clipped quotations to Charlie or Burr, which does not affect the book-level person.
